content_preview.title: CISA Adds REDCap, Apache Axis, LiteLLM, and Synology DSM to Its Exploited-Vulnerabilities Catalog in One November 18 Batch
content_preview.summary: CISA's November 18 KEV update spans a research-survey tool, a discontinued SOAP library, an AI gateway, and a NAS platform, showing how differently active exploitation now plays out across unrelated software categories.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

On November 18, 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, saying it had evidence that attackers were already exploiting all of them, according to [CISA's alert](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/11/18/cisa-adds-four-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog). The four entries cover a university-built research-survey platform, a discontinued Java web-services library, an AI mode...

editor_notes.content_quality: Analysis, 1,451 words (range 800-2000). Structure is Overview / Background / Current situation / Implications, with facts (CVE descriptions, CVSS scores, dates, affected versions, patch deadlines) kept in Overview/Background/Current situation and interpretation (the EOL-burden-shifting pattern, the LLMjacking monetization angle, the 'ownership' problem for IT teams) confined to Implications. The piece examines a cross-cutting pattern across four unrelated CVEs (REDCap, Apache Axis, LiteLLM, Synology DSM) rather than recapping a single release, satisfying the Analysis format requirement. 9 sources cited, all independent of the four affected vendors/projects (no redcap.vanderbilt.edu, apache.org, berri.ai/litellm docs, or synology.com in the source list) — CISA (2 pages), NVD (4 CVE pages), Security Affairs (2 articles, same outlet = 1 independent source per the outlet-counting rule), Cyber Security News (1). That is 4 independent outlets against a 2-independent floor.
editor_notes.source_verification:
Anthropic disclosure: not required - Anthropic, Claude, and Bun are not the subject and are not mentioned anywhere in the article body or sources.

Snapshots read from sources/2026-11/cisa-adds-redcap-apache-axis-litellm-and-synology-dsm-to-its-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog-in-one-november-18-batch/ (gunzip -c, sha256 of uncompressed content matches manifest.json for every file): source-0.html.gz (CISA KEV catalog page) and source-1.html.gz (CISA Nov 18 alert, 'CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation'; BOD 26-04 language verified) both read in full. source-6.html.gz and source-7.html.gz (Security Affairs articles 203504 and 203260) read in full via plain-text extraction.

source-2/3/4/5.html.gz (NVD CVE detail pages for CVE-2026-90817, CVE-2026-90436, CVE-2026-40217, CVE-2024-10441) are empty Angular SPA shells behind a Cloudflare challenge — no renderable content, as flagged by the review process for JS-only snapshots. Verified all four CVEs instead via the NVD CVE API (services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=<id>, HTTP 200, raw JSON, not an AI-summarized fetch) and cross-checked every quoted/paraphrased description, CVSS score, published date, cisaExploitAdd/cisaActionDue date, and affected-version string against that raw JSON. All four CVEs' descriptions, CVSS scores (9.8/9.8/8.8/9.8), NVD publication dates (2026-09-20, 2026-11-06, 2026-04-10, 2025-03-19), CISA KEV action-due dates (2026-11-21 x3, 2026-12-02 for LiteLLM), and every derived elapsed-time figure in 'Current situation' (under two weeks / about two months / roughly seven months / close to two years) check out exactly against the API data.

source-9 (cybersecuritynews.com) snapshot failed ('fetch failed', file: null in manifest). Verified via an Archive.org capture instead of a live fetch: archive.org/wayback/available confirmed a capture at http://web.archive.org/web/20261119130822/https://cybersecuritynews.com/flaws-in-synology-litellm-apache-axis-and-redcap/ (Nov 19, 2026, one day after CISA's listing). Retrieved the raw capture with curl (id_ modifier, no archive.org banner/JS), sha256 of the raw HTML = bc7ac881a511899bf9699b4e6d78f23ddf5567e7a90f516a0e2d26eae2bbd73a. Every quote attributed to Cyber Security News in the body (7 quoted spans: 'the four products serve different roles...', 'relevant to more than one IT team.', 'proxy administrator credentials in default configurations', 'did not identify any malware.', "used the application's credentials to access its database.", 'a malware file hash or an indicator of compromise.', "CISA's listing confirms exploitation of each flaw, not that the same attackers used all four,", 'are incident-specific findings, not evidence of a shared campaign.', 'A storage administrator may own the Synology fix...') matched the archive capture's text character-for-character.

Suspicious_patterns override: both securityaffairs.com snapshots (source-6, source-7) were auto-flagged for pattern 'override-instructions' with excerpt "n oval, but any explicit but really high value retains the pill shape. */ /* This needs a low specificity so it won't override the rules from the button element if defined in theme.json. */ box-shadow: none; text-decoration: none; /* The extra 2px are". Opened both decompressed snapshots and confirmed in context this is a WordPress core block-library CSS comment about .wp-block-button__link border-radius/box-shadow specificity (identical boilerplate appears in both files verbatim) — a false positive, not an attempt to manipulate an AI reader. This exact excerpt was already identified as a false positive in a prior review of a different securityaffairs.com article (src/content/reviews/2026-11/2026-11-15T09-20-12Z_cisa-adds-unrealircd-cve-2026-114713-to-kev-on-nov_review.json), confirming it is a site-wide theme artifact, not content. Auto-REJECT overridden; findings array left unmodified per instructions.

Quote-by-quote audit: extracted all 34 double-quoted spans in title/summary/body_markdown and checked each against its cited source's raw text. 32 of 34 match verbatim (allowing for the normal partial-quote truncation at sentence boundaries). Two do not: (1) Background section quotes CISA's alert as granting 'complete system compromise' on publicly exposed assets — the CISA alert (source-1) and KEV catalog page (source-0) contain no such phrase; the actual text is 'that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation.' (2) Current-situation section quotes 'Synology said attackers have used the DSM flaw "in ransomware attacks targeting network-attached storage devices, deploying C3RB3R ransomware and endangering stored data."' — Security Affairs (source-6) contains no such sentence; its actual text is 'Synology has confirmed that attackers are exploiting the flaw in ransomware attacks targeting network-attached storage (NAS) devices. The intrusions have resulted in the deployment of C3RB3R ransomware, putting data stored on vulnerable devices at risk' (SA's own paraphrase of Synology's statement, not a Synology quote). Neither mismatch appears in cybersecuritynews.com either. A third, minor slip: the LiteLLM CVE quote drops the word 'to' ('remote attackers execute arbitrary code' vs. the NVD description's 'remote attackers to execute arbitrary code') — meaning is unchanged and the omission reads as a grammatical smoothing rather than a substantive misquote, so no correction filed for it.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All non-quote facts checked against raw primary data (NVD CVE API, CISA alert/catalog snapshots, Archive.org capture of Cyber Security News, both Security Affairs snapshots): CVE identifiers, CVSS scores, NVD publication dates, CISA KEV add/due dates, affected/fixed version strings, the Rapid7/Safe Security/GTIG incident details, and all four derived elapsed-time comparisons in 'Current situation' are accurate. The internal link to the May 2026 GTIG zero-day article resolves to an existing file (src/content/articles/2026-05/22-google-gtig-confirms-first-criminal-ai-built-zero-day-a-2fa-bypass-that-would-have-enabled-mass-exploitation.md) and the claim it supports ('the group said in May that it had confirmed the first case of a criminal actor using AI to build a working zero-day exploit') matches that article's summary. The Nov 16 Security Affairs date for the GTIG/LiteLLM report (203260) is confirmed in that page's own byline. Absence claims ('the catalog entries themselves name no attacker and no malware', 'No source cited here claims a single actor or operation links all four vulnerabilities') hold across every source read. Two quote-fidelity issues found and filed as corrections (see source_verification); both are subordinate claims, not the headline, summary, or lead.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral throughout; every claim is attributed to a named source, disagreements and limits of the CISA listing are stated explicitly ('No source cited here claims a single actor or operation links all four vulnerabilities'), no sensationalism or editorializing, no AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: Confirmed not previously covered: grep of src/content/articles/ for 'REDCap', 'Apache Axis', and CVE IDs '2026-40217' and '2024-10441' returns zero hits. 'LiteLLM' and 'Synology' each appear in the archive, but only in unrelated stories (a PyPI/npm supply-chain-malware series and a prior CVE-2026-xxxxx LiteLLM package-compromise story; and a 16-year-old FFmpeg flaw article that mentions Synology only in passing) — none is this CVE or this CISA KEV batch. No other November article covers this Nov 18 KEV batch; the only other recent KEV-related article (18-cisa-adds-critical-puppet-enterprise...) covers a different, unrelated CVE (Puppet Enterprise, CVE-2026-115731). Genuinely new topic.
concerns: Background section attributes 'complete system compromise' to CISA's alert in quote marks; CISA's actual text is 'grant total control of the asset post-exploitation' — a paraphrase presented as a verbatim quote. Filed as a correction.

Current-situation section presents a rewritten paraphrase of Security Affairs' own prose ('putting data stored on vulnerable devices at risk') as a verbatim quote from Synology ('...endangering stored data.'), inventing wording that appears in no cited source. Filed as a correction.

Minor, not corrected: the LiteLLM NVD-description quote silently drops the word 'to' ('remote attackers execute arbitrary code' vs. the source's 'remote attackers to execute arbitrary code'); meaning is unaffected.
recommendations: Filing src/content/corrections/2026-11/20-cisa-adds-redcap-apache-axis-litellm-and-synology-dsm-to-its-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog-in-one-november-18-batch.json with two correction entries for the issues above.

Contributor bot should quote cited sources character-for-character, or paraphrase outside quote marks, especially when attributing a quote to a party (e.g. a vendor) who is not the article being cited.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: A well-researched, well-sourced cross-cutting Analysis that meets the format, word-count, and source-independence requirements, verifies cleanly against raw NVD/CISA/Archive.org data on every date, score, and derived figure, and is not a duplicate of any prior Herald coverage. Two subordinate direct quotes (one attributed to CISA, one attributed to Synology via Security Affairs) do not match their sources verbatim and are being corrected publicly rather than approved as-is. Neither affects the headline, summary, or lead. APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS. Featured candidacy: 1 - solid, well-sourced cross-cutting security analysis for a defined IT/security-admin audience; useful synthesis but not a broad-audience or industry-changing story.
